newsitem.title: FRANCE: Aerospace firms eye Europe industry consolidation.
newsitem.headline: Aerospace firms eye Europe industry consolidation.

text.p: Europe's big aerospace firms, threatened by U.S. giants, are considering prospects for integrating their civilian and military businesses, industry sources and analysts told Reuters.

But talks are complicated by France's election of a Socialist government opposed to privatisations that are vital for consolidation of the defence industry. Germany's budget problems may also threaten its role in the joint Eurofighter programme.

Executives from France's Aerospatiale, British Aerospace Plc (BAe), Daimler-Benz Aerospace (Dasa) of Germany and Construcciones Aeronauticas SA (Casa) of Spain met in Paris last week on the fringes of talks by members of the Airbus group, the sources said.

The firms are partners in Airbus Industrie. But they were looking at wider strategic issues stemming from mergers between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, Raytheon and Hughes Electronics Corp, and the giant Lockheed Martin.

The U.S. mergers will mean an effective "doubling" of research funds for American companies, whereas European industry has to share scarce money between six or 10 firms, an aerospace executive said, asking not to be identified.

"Dasa said the European aerospace industry has to go beyond a restructuring of Airbus. There has to be a European grouping, with Airbus as a part of it," he said. "Airbus on its own cannot face up to the vitality and appetite of the Americans," said the source.
Dasa took the initiative last week to broaden the talks on Airbus restructuring, he added.
A separate aerospace source said: "The Airbus restructuring was never meant to be the be-all and end-all of European integration and Dasa probably wanted to re-emphasise the point."
But while the need to integrate in Europe may be pressing, the reality is that Europe lacks the legal framework for a transnational company and common rules on tax, social security and state support.
Any integration of the military and civilian arms would need to maintain national firms under a holding group.
The second aerospace source said merger talks reported to have started between BAe and Dasa were likely to be complicated by Bonn's difficulties in funding its share in the Eurofighter combat plane.

Germany's Eurofighter financing has been hit by the Bonn government's struggle to bring its budget deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product, to meet the terms for joining a single European currency by 1999.
Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain are partners in the 40-billion pound ($65.3 billion) Eurofighter programme, which could provide the platform for integrating the military wings of BAe and Dasa.
But Bonn needs to release the next tranche of financing to keep Dasa up to speed with its industrial partners.

In France, consolidation is on hold as the incoming Socialists have not confirmed plans to merge Aerospatiale with warplane maker Dassault Aviation, and whether the Aerospatiale/Dassault group will be privatised.

BAe and Dasa enjoy greater autonomy as they are private companies and also share work on Airbus and Eurofighter programmes. Aerospatiale is state-constrolled and has no military aircraft interests other than in helicopters.
Aerospatiale derives most of its sales from Airbus and is counting on Dassault to give it the military arm which will make it an equal in any talks with BAe and Dasa.
The Socialists have indicated hostility to privatisations, which could mean the effective renationalisation of Dassault and hamper Aerospatiale's ability to keep up with BAe and Dasa.
There are also fears the Socialists will cancel the sale of the state's 58 percent in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, which was also seen as vital to consolidation.
Conglomerate Lagardere is also waiting to see if its plans to ally with Dasa in space and missiles will get French government approval. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
